title: Verifiable Environments for AI in Biology — Kenny Workman, LatchBio

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building benchmarks (SpatialBench with 146 problems, long-horizon tasks, biosecurity evals), evaluation methodology (human verification, rubric-based grading, choke-point nodes), and measurement design for AI in biology. The speaker frames the entire effort around how to measure whether AI agents can do real biological work—verifiability, durability across analysis paths, task ambiguity, and the distinction between reasoning and memorized knowledge. This is fundamentally about how quality is measured rather than how a single system is built.

secondary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
secondary.rationale: LatchBio adapted coding models into biology agents, built agent prototypes, and discusses agent trajectories from real scientists. The talk covers how agents interact with large experimental data files and iterate with scientists, and how agent capability gaps (between knowing biology and writing code) are evaluated.

secondary.label: AI Data Engineering
secondary.rationale: The talk involves building evaluation datasets as data products (SpatialBench, preclinical pharmacology benchmark), working with massive biological datasets (2–7 TB per run), and constructing benchmark data nodes with deterministic graders. Dataset construction as an engineering discipline is a recurring theme.

secondary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
secondary.rationale: A significant section covers biosecurity evaluation: LatchBio acquired a biosecurity company, built red team tasks encoding harmful biological structure, and found model refusals create an asymmetric evaluation problem. While framed primarily as an evaluation challenge, it has clear safety and governance dimensions.

domains.label: Scientific Research
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about AI for scientific research: building benchmarks and agents for biology, evaluating frontier models on scientific tasks, and treating experimental biology as a verifiable substrate for AI training. LatchBio operates as a vertical AI lab for science.

domains.label: Healthcare & Life Sciences
domains.rationale: LatchBio works in pharma, drug discovery, spatial biology, and preclinical pharmacology. The talk covers omics experiment types, go/no-go drug decisions, and a first preclinical pharmacology benchmark for small molecules.

domains.label: Security & Defense
domains.rationale: Biosecurity evaluation is a notable subtopic: red team tasks encoding harmful biological structure, model refusal behavior, and work with American Wetware and Aquid on biosecurity evaluation.

summary: Kenny Workman, co-founder and CTO of LatchBio, presents experimental biology as a verifiable substrate for training AI agents. Biology generates enormous datasets (single cell 2–6 TB/run, spatial 7 TB/run) that exceed manual inspection. LatchBio evolved from a pharma data tool vendor into a vertical AI lab for benchmark and agent engineering. They adapted coding models into biology agents and built SpatialBench (146 problems, later revised to 159) spanning spatial biology kits and analysis DAG tasks with deterministic Python graders modeled on SWEET-bench. Frontier models cannot yet be trusted for real biological work (20–38% base accuracy), lacking the capability to extract scientific insight from real-world data. Good biological tests must be verifiable, durable across valid analysis paths, and require data interaction rather than memorized knowledge. Human verification by 6 domain experts over two rounds produced 115 verified tasks, revealing that ambiguous prompts (open choices in normalization, radius, gene splitting) and arbitrary numerical QC thresholds quietly make benchmarks uninformative. LatchBio built long-horizon tasks (SpatialBench-Long, 24 evaluations) simulating entire paper result sections; no models solve these yet (top score 11.1%). Verifiable end rewards are uninformative for long-horizon tasks, so they use rubrics built from invariant choke-point nodes in the analysis DAG, though these correlate only loosely with verifiable outcomes. They are expanding benchmarks across omics types (EpiBench, scBench) and drug discovery (TxBench-PP), and addressing biosecurity evaluation (BioSecBench-Refusal: 61 Routine + 46 Red-Team tasks) where model refusals create an evaluation problem—routine tasks are refused at comparable or higher rates than red-team tasks. The overall effort is a flywheel: better benchmarks drive better models, which improve products deployed via agent.bio serving 300+ biopharmas.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a coherent system: the verifiable substrate concept (biology as executable, checkable code) motivates deterministic grading functions and analysis DAGs, which in turn require durability across valid analysis paths to avoid false negatives. When end-outcome grading becomes too sparse for long-horizon tasks, choke-point rubrics and human verification extend the evaluation framework. The AI concepts—agentic biology, coding model adaptation, and the frontier model capability gap—define what is being measured, while the benchmark flywheel, biosecurity evaluation, and model refusal asymmetry show how measurement drives both model improvement and safety. Together they illustrate a complete methodology for building domain-specific AI evaluation: from substrate identification through benchmark construction, human verification, rubric design, and safety auditing, all feeding a commercial-productive flywheel.
temporalContext: The talk was published on July 31, 2026. LatchBio was founded circa 2021 at UC Berkeley. SpatialBench was originally published as an arXiv preprint on December 26, 2025 with 146 problems, later revised to 159 problems. Human verification results were published May 29, 2026. SpatialBench-Long was published May 27, 2026. BioSecBench-Refusal was published July 6, 2026. The TwentyTwo acquisition occurred June 29, 2026. GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7 model evaluation results were published April 29, 2026. Research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. The talk references model trajectory data from January to March 2026 model releases.
takeaways: Biology generates enormous experimental datasets (2–7 TB per run) that exceed manual inspection, making it a natural substrate for AI agents.
LatchBio treats experimental biology as a verifiable substrate analogous to code for software, where data analysis provides ground-truth checkable outcomes.
Frontier coding models adapted to biology show early promise but cannot yet be trusted for real scientific work; they lack the capability to extract insight from real-world data.
SpatialBench contains 146 problems spanning spatial biology kits and analysis pipeline tasks, borrowing structural ideas from SWEET-bench.
Good biological tests must be verifiable, durable across valid analysis paths, and require data interaction rather than memorized knowledge.
Human verification revealed ambiguous task prompts and arbitrary numerical QC thresholds that quietly make benchmarks uninformative.
Long-horizon tasks simulating full paper result sections or drug go/no-go decisions take a week for three people each to build; no models solve them yet.
Rubric-based grading using invariant choke-point nodes in analysis trees is being explored but correlates only loosely with verifiable outcomes.
LatchBio is expanding benchmarks across omics types and into drug discovery, with a first preclinical pharmacology benchmark for small molecules.
Biosecurity evaluation shows model refusals are their own problem: routine tasks get used drastically more frequently than red team tasks.

concepts.name: Agentic Biology
concepts.explanation: AI agents that interact with large experimental datasets (2–7 TB per run), write code, and reason scientifically about biological data. LatchBio adapted frontier coding models into biology agents without domain-specific post-training.
concepts.importance: Represents the application of coding agent architectures to a new domain with unique challenges: massive data volumes, multi-step analysis pipelines, and the need for scientific reasoning beyond code execution.

concepts.name: Coding Model Adaptation
concepts.explanation: Using frontier coding models designed for software engineering as biology agents, exploiting their code-writing and tool-use capabilities while revealing domain-specific gaps in scientific reasoning.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates both the transferability of agentic capabilities and the specific capability gap between knowing biology and extracting scientific insight from real-world data.

concepts.name: Frontier Model Capability Gap
concepts.explanation: The specific gap between knowing biology and writing code versus extracting scientific insight from real-world data. Frontier models remain at 20–38% accuracy on SpatialBench; GPT-5.5 is flat versus GPT-5.4 (57.65% vs 57.44%).
concepts.importance: Identifies where current models fail and what benchmarks should measure, guiding both evaluation design and model development priorities.

concepts.name: Benchmark Flywheel
concepts.explanation: A feedback loop where better benchmarks drive better frontier models (benchmarks appear in Anthropic model cards), which improve LatchBio's products, which fund better benchmarks. Open, reproducible evaluation on benchmarks.bio reinforces the cycle.
concepts.importance: Strategic model for sustained evaluation-driven improvement, linking open benchmark publication to commercial product improvement and frontier lab competition.

concepts.name: Biosecurity Evaluation
concepts.explanation: Measuring model refusal behavior on routine versus red-team biology tasks, where red-team tasks look innocuous but encode harmful biological structure (e.g., a GFP clone that is actually a toxin). Refusals are framed as an evaluation problem, not just a safety feature.
concepts.importance: Reveals that safety misalignment (over-refusal) blocks legitimate research while the refusal mechanism fails to selectively distinguish routine from hazardous tasks.

concepts.name: Model Refusal Asymmetry
concepts.explanation: Routine biology tasks are refused at comparable or higher rates than concealed threat tasks. Across 16 model-harness configurations, refusal rates ranged 7–74% on Routine vs 1–62% on Red-Team, with Routine and Red-Team rates correlated at r=0.91.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that refusal triggers are surface-level text patterns rather than semantic understanding of biological risk, undermining the effectiveness of refusal-based safety mechanisms.

concepts.name: Rubric-Based Grading for RL
concepts.explanation: Using choke-point rubrics as reward signals for reinforcement learning and benchmarking, despite their loose correlation with verifiable end outcomes. The correlation is insufficient for full confidence in RL settings.
concepts.importance: Addresses the fundamental gap between sparse binary end-outcome rewards and the informative intermediate signals needed for effective RL training on complex tasks.

concepts.name: Spatial Biology Benchmarking
concepts.explanation: Domain-specific benchmarks for spatial transcriptomics spanning 5 platforms (Curio, Vizgen, Xenium, AtlasXOmics, Visium) and 7 task categories with deterministic graders, originally 146 problems revised to 159.
concepts.importance: First benchmark of its kind for a high-data-volume biology modality; establishes the template for verifiable, data-interaction-requiring evaluation in experimental biology.

concepts.name: Omics Benchmark Expansion
concepts.explanation: Systematic benchmark construction extending beyond spatial biology to single-cell (scBench), epigenomics (EpiBench), and drug discovery (TxBench-PP), indexing the full program landscape from discovery through development.
concepts.importance: Extends evaluation methodology across the biology research pipeline, creating comprehensive coverage that prevents overfitting to a single modality.

concepts.name: Preclinical Pharmacology Benchmarking
concepts.explanation: TxBench-PP benchmark covering potency, mechanism, exposure, safety, and efficacy decisions for small-molecule preclinical pharmacology, bridging biology AI evaluation into drug discovery pipelines.
concepts.importance: Connects AI agent evaluation to concrete go/no-go drug development decisions, demonstrating practical commercial and clinical relevance of benchmark engineering.

concepts.name: Deterministic Grading Functions
concepts.explanation: Python function graders modeled on SWEET-bench that verify agent outputs on data nodes, enabling automated, reproducible evaluation without per-run human judgment.
concepts.importance: Foundation of verifiable benchmarks in any domain; makes automated evaluation pipelines possible and ensures results are reproducible across model versions and harness configurations.

concepts.name: Analysis DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)
concepts.explanation: Multi-step biological data analysis pipelines represented as DAGs where each node produces a verifiable intermediate output. When end-outcome grading is too sparse, tasks are broken into DAG components for component-level grading.
concepts.importance: Structural decomposition enables granular evaluation of multi-step agent workflows, bridging the gap between single-step benchmarks and real-world scientific analysis.

concepts.name: Benchmark Engineering
concepts.explanation: The discipline of designing evaluation datasets that are verifiable, durable, and require genuine data interaction rather than memorized knowledge, extending principles from SWE-bench and SWEET-bench to new domains.
concepts.importance: Transfers proven software engineering evaluation methodologies to scientific domains, establishing reusable patterns for domain-specific benchmark construction.

concepts.name: Durability Across Valid Analysis Paths
concepts.explanation: A benchmark property ensuring tasks do not incorrectly fail valid alternative analysis approaches. Science lacks canonical ground truth, so lazy construction can fail valid solutions and silently make benchmarks uninformative.
concepts.importance: Without durability, benchmarks produce false negatives that erode trust and mislead model development, particularly in domains where multiple valid methods exist.

concepts.name: Choke-Point Rubrics
concepts.explanation: Rubric-based grading using invariant nodes in an analysis DAG that must be correctly traversed regardless of the analysis path chosen. Used when verifiable end-outcome rewards are uninformative for long-horizon tasks.
concepts.importance: Enables partial-credit evaluation for complex multi-step tasks where binary pass/fail is too sparse, though the loose correlation with verifiable outcomes remains an open challenge for RL and benchmarking confidence.

concepts.name: Human Verification in Benchmark Design
concepts.explanation: Using domain experts to solve benchmark tasks and identify ambiguities, serving as the best proxy for ground truth in domains lacking canonical answers. LatchBio used 6 domain experts across two rounds to produce a verified subset.
concepts.importance: Reveals task design flaws that automated verification cannot catch, and forces more rigorous reasoning than self-grading, ultimately determining whether a benchmark is informative.

concepts.name: Task Ambiguity Detection
concepts.explanation: Open choices in task prompts—such as normalization method, radius selection, and gene list splitting—that silently make benchmarks uninformative by admitting multiple valid interpretations with different correct answers.
concepts.importance: A fundamental threat to benchmark validity that requires human verification to detect; ambiguous tasks create noise that masks real model capability differences.

concepts.name: Long-Horizon Task Design
concepts.explanation: Benchmark tasks simulating entire paper result sections or go/no-go drug decisions, requiring multi-step workflows across multiple experiment types and contextual interpretation. Each task took a team of three approximately one week to construct.
concepts.importance: Tests capabilities beyond single-step reasoning and stays ahead of rapidly improving frontier models; reveals the gap between component-level and end-to-end scientific reasoning.

concepts.name: Verifiable Substrate
concepts.explanation: Treating code and data analysis as an executable, checkable layer in biology analogous to code for software, providing ground-truth feedback signals for AI training.
concepts.importance: Makes biology tractable for AI agent development by establishing that measurement-grounded data analysis is the executable, feedback-rich layer where agents can be trained and evaluated.

sections.title: Motivation: Data volumes in biology
sections.summary: Workman introduces LatchBio as a vertical AI lab and motivates agents in biology by showing the log-linear growth of experimental data, driven by single cell biology, spatial biology, and proteomics. Single cell runs yield 2–6 TB, spatial 7 TB, proteomics hundreds of GB, exceeding consumer laptop storage.

sections.title: Decomposing biology papers into tasks
sections.summary: Modern biology research follows a pattern: choose a biological model, generate data, process it, reason in context of prior literature, make a claim. Workman frames this as panning for signal in noise, and argues that code and data analysis scaffold biology into an executable, verifiable substrate for training, analogous to code for software.

sections.title: LatchBio history and agent prototypes
sections.summary: LatchBio started five years ago at Berkeley as a data tool vendor for pharma, then shifted to white-labeled software for kit builders. Around last summer, agent prototypes built on coding models began working, handling large experimental data files and iterating with scientists on questions like gene overexpression in malignant versus non-malignant tissue.

sections.title: Frontier models cannot be trusted yet
sections.summary: Despite early promise, frontier models cannot be trusted for real biological work. They lack the capability between knowing biology and writing code—specifically extracting scientific insight from real-world data, which also requires data analysis and domain reasoning.

sections.title: Sequencing-based spatial biology
sections.summary: LatchBio chose spatial biology as a greenfield starting point. Sequencing-based spatial capture uses slides of DNA-coated beads that fuse to tissue RNA, capturing geometric resolution of RNA distribution. Output is a large matrix of numbers and a high-content image, processed through variable steps with little field consensus.

sections.title: Building SpatialBench
sections.summary: Existing benchmarks measured Q&A or were not focused on experiment types, so LatchBio built SpatialBench with 146 problems spanning kits and analysis DAG tasks. Each evaluation includes data nodes, a task prompt, grader configuration, and a deterministic Python grader. End-outcome grading was too sparse, so tasks were broken into DAG components.

sections.title: Properties of good biological tests
sections.summary: Good biological tests must be verifiable with deterministic functions, durable across valid analysis paths, and require data interaction rather than memorized knowledge. Durability is critical because science lacks clear ground truth—lazy construction can incorrectly fail valid analysis paths.

sections.title: Human verification and task ambiguity
sections.summary: Human verification became essential after trajectory data from January to March model releases revealed bad assumptions. In science's absence of canonical answers, scientists grading each other's work served as the best proxy. A concrete example shows ambiguity in splitting gene lists, defining inflammatory genes, choosing radius, and normalizing data—issues only revealed through human verification.

sections.title: Verified subset and arbitrary QC thresholds
sections.summary: Workman notes that canonical numerical QC thresholds in bioinformatics are often arbitrary, and that evaluation forces more rigorous reasoning than doing the task yourself. After two rounds of human attempts, LatchBio produced and published a verified subset of the benchmark.

sections.title: Long-horizon benchmark tasks
sections.summary: To stay ahead of frontier labs, LatchBio built longer-horizon tasks that simulate result sections of entire papers or go/no-go drug decisions. These use whole workflows, multiple experiment types, and require contextual interpretation. Each took a week for three people to construct. An example task asks whether an agent can reconstruct a metastatic niche from tumor and metastatic biopsies. No models solve these yet. Verifiable end rewards are uninformative, so they are experimenting with rubrics built from invariant choke-point nodes, though these correlate only loosely with verifiable outcomes.

sections.title: Expansion across omics and drug discovery
sections.summary: LatchBio is expanding beyond spatial biology to other omics classes—single-cell, epigenomics—and into drug discovery. Benchmarks now appear in Anthropic model cards. They published a first preclinical pharmacology benchmark for small molecules and are systematically indexing the program landscape from discovery through development and translation, stratified by therapeutic and experiment types.

sections.title: Biosecurity and refusals as evaluation
sections.summary: LatchBio acquired a biosecurity company and released work with American Wetware and Aquid. Biology model refusals are framed as an evaluation problem: models refuse basic biology questions. They built routine scientist tasks and red team tasks that look innocuous but encode harmful structure (e.g., a GFP clone that is actually a toxin or virus bootstrapper). Routine tasks were used drastically more frequently than red team tasks, which is not great.

sections.title: Flywheel and closing
sections.summary: Workman frames the effort as a research lab doing both research and deployment. They work with kit manufacturers to inform benchmark design, encourage labs to compete on benchmarks to improve models for their products, and describe this as a rewarding flywheel. LatchBio is hiring aggressively across engineering and science.

organization.name: LatchBio
organization.summary: LatchBio is a San Francisco-based vertical AI lab founded in 2021 that builds verifiable benchmarks and deploys AI agents for biology. The company evolved from a pharma data tool vendor into a research lab focused on benchmark engineering across spatial biology, single-cell biology, epigenomics, preclinical pharmacology, and biosecurity. LatchBio built SpatialBench (146 problems), SpatialBench-Long, EpiBench, TxBench-PP, and BioSecBench benchmarks, deploys agents via agent.bio supporting 40+ solution providers and 300+ biopharmas and R&D labs, and hosts live reproducible results at benchmarks.bio. On June 29, 2026, LatchBio acquired TwentyTwo to form its Latch Biosecurity division. The company has approximately 29 employees and $163.2M in total funding.
organization.status: Active - independent company, hiring aggressively across engineering and science, actively deploying benchmarks and agents

technologies.label: SpatialBench Benchmark System
technologies.summary: SpatialBench is a benchmark for agentic spatial biology data analysis, originally with 146 problems (revised to 159) across 5 spatial platforms (Curio, Vizgen, Xenium, AtlasXOmics, Visium) and 7 task categories (Dimensionality Reduction, Cell Typing, Normalization, Differential Expression, Clustering, QC, Spatial Analysis). Each problem includes experimental data, a task prompt, grader configuration, and a deterministic Python grader modeled on SWEET-bench. Good biological tests must be verifiable with deterministic functions, durable across valid analysis paths, and require data interaction rather than memorized knowledge. Human verification by 6 domain experts over two rounds produced 115 verified tasks, revealing that ambiguous task prompts (open choices in normalization, radius, gene splitting) and arbitrary numerical QC thresholds silently make benchmarks uninformative. Base model accuracy remains low at 20-38%.
technologies.role: Core benchmark technology; the primary artifact discussed in the majority of the talk. Demonstrates how to build verifiable, durable biological benchmarks with deterministic graders, analysis DAG decomposition, and human verification. Establishes the template for all subsequent LatchBio benchmarks.

technologies.label: SpatialBench-Long & Choke-Point Rubrics
technologies.summary: SpatialBench-Long is a long-horizon benchmark with 24 evaluations across PDAC, glioblastoma organoids, Cas9 lineage-traced lung adenocarcinoma, and mouse optic nerve systems. Tasks simulate entire paper result sections or go/no-go drug decisions, requiring multi-step workflows across multiple experiment types and contextual interpretation. Each task took approximately a week for three people to construct. No models solve these tasks yet; the top score is 8/72 runs (11.1%). Because verifiable end-outcome rewards are uninformative for long-horizon tasks, LatchBio developed rubric-based grading using invariant choke-point nodes in the analysis DAG, though these correlate only loosely with verifiable outcomes, limiting confidence for RL and benchmarking.
technologies.role: Extends benchmark methodology to long-horizon tasks; demonstrates the gap between component-level and end-to-end scientific reasoning. Introduces choke-point rubrics as a novel partial-credit evaluation approach for complex multi-step tasks where binary pass/fail is uninformative.

technologies.label: BioSecBench-Refusal
technologies.summary: BioSecBench-Refusal is a biosecurity evaluation benchmark pairing 61 Routine tasks with 46 Red-Team tasks that look innocuous but encode harmful biological structure (e.g., a GFP clone that is actually a toxin or virus bootstrapper). Across 16 model-harness configurations, refusal rates ranged 7-74% on Routine vs 1-62% on Red-Team, with Routine and Red-Team rates correlated at r=0.91. This reveals that refusal triggers are surface-level text patterns rather than semantic understanding of biological risk, making model refusals an evaluation problem where routine tasks are used drastically more frequently than red-team tasks. The benchmark was a collaboration between LatchBio and American Wetware, with 107 evaluations written by 14 subject-matter experts covering microbiology, virology, immunology, plant biology, and synthetic biology.
technologies.role: Biosecurity evaluation benchmark; the third major benchmark discussed in the talk. Reveals that model refusals are miscalibrated and constitute an evaluation problem where routine tasks are refused at comparable or higher rates than concealed threats. Built in collaboration with American Wetware after LatchBio acquired TwentyTwo to form Latch Biosecurity.

technologies.label: Benchmark Flywheel & Expansion Platform
technologies.summary: LatchBio operates a benchmark-and-deployment flywheel: open, reproducible benchmark results on benchmarks.bio drive frontier lab competition (benchmarks appear in Anthropic model cards), which improves models, which improves LatchBio's agent products deployed via agent.bio serving 300+ biopharmas. The benchmark portfolio is systematically expanding beyond spatial biology across omics types (EpiBench for epigenomics, scBench for single-cell) and into drug discovery (TxBench-PP for preclinical pharmacology), indexing the full program landscape from discovery through development, stratified by therapeutic and experiment types. The flywheel connects open benchmark publication to commercial product improvement and frontier lab competition.
technologies.role: Platform and expansion strategy; the closing framing of the talk. The flywheel connects open benchmark publication to frontier lab competition and commercial agent deployment. The expansion portfolio shows the approach generalizing beyond spatial biology to other omics types and drug discovery.

evidence.excerpt: Single cell experiments can yield two to six terabytes per run. Spatial runs can yield seven terabytes of run.
evidence.supports: Biology generates terabyte-scale experimental data per run.

evidence.excerpt: frontier models cannot be trusted to do real work. They're missing some capability between knowing biology and writing code.
evidence.supports: Frontier models lack capability to extract scientific insight from real-world biological data.

evidence.excerpt: It's called spatial bench. Um last December, there's 146 problems.
evidence.supports: LatchBio built SpatialBench with 146 benchmark problems.

evidence.excerpt: Science does not admit clear ground truth. Um if you are lazy with your ground truth construction of the task, a possible valid analysis path can come with the correct answer, um and you'll fail it incorrectly.
evidence.supports: Durability across analysis paths is critical because biology lacks clear ground truth.

evidence.excerpt: a lot of people in bioinformatics canonically have used like numerical thresholds to QC stuff. Just like completely arbitrary stuff.
evidence.supports: Canonical numerical QC thresholds in bioinformatics are often arbitrary and not durable.

evidence.excerpt: can an agent reconstruct a like metastatic niche in a tumor? ... can it use like both the genetics and mRNA of the metastatic lesions and the tumor to like find the part of the tumor that initially seeded the metastatic growth
evidence.supports: LatchBio built long-horizon tasks such as reconstructing a metastatic niche from tumor and metastatic biopsies.

evidence.excerpt: None of the models get this right. Um but they're getting there.
evidence.supports: No frontier models solve the long-horizon metastatic niche task yet.

evidence.excerpt: verifiable reward at the end are like somewhat uninformative ... they're loosely correlated numerically, um making us not fully have confidence in them for things like RL or benchmarking.
evidence.supports: Rubric-based choke-point grading correlates only loosely with verifiable outcomes, limiting confidence for RL and benchmarking.

evidence.excerpt: we found that the routine tasks like drastic get drastic used drastically more frequently than the red team tasks, which is uh not great.
evidence.supports: Biology model refusals cause routine tasks to be used drastically more frequently than red team tasks.
